title: Hosted API demo - chat/text generation basics
meeting_header:
Date: 2025-07-02
Time: 15:00 - 15:45 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Evan Parker (Redwood AE); Samantha Li (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (NexaHead ML); Carlos Mendes (Eng Manager); Jing Wu (Security); Tom Kelley (Product)
summary: Redwood AE/SE demo of Hosted API focused on chat and text-generation basics: streaming responses, core parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry patterns, SDK usage, and Console walkthrough. Customer (NexaHealth) is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a chat assistant in healthcare workflows; primary concerns are latency, cost, PHI handling, and SOC2/SSO. Next steps: send pricing, share security & SOC2 docs, schedule a performance pilot and follow-up POC scoping call.
transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick intro then dive into the hosted API demo. Uh Samantha and I will show chat and text generation basics, streaming, params and retries.
[00:12] Priya: Great, yeah we were hoping to see how the streaming works since we need sub-second tokens for the agent UI.
[00:20] Samantha: Cool, we'll start with the REST and SDK flow. Quick qual question — what's your current stack? Are you using OpenAI endpoints or self-hosted models?
[00:33] Carlos: We're prototyping with OpenAI for now but want to move off or have fallback. Latency is a big one, and cost, obviously.
[00:40] Evan: Totally. Hosted API gives you fast onboarding; we also have Dedicated if you need predictable capacity. For this demo we'll use a hosted model variant and show streaming.
[01:10] Samantha: Ok sharing my screen — here's a sample chat request. We set model, messages array, temperature, max_tokens and a streaming flag. Note you can stream with server-sent events or WebSocket.
[01:32] Tom: Do you support function calling or structured outputs?
[01:36] Samantha: Yes we do function/tool calling, though in hosted demos we focus on plain chat. Function calling is supported with structured JSON outputs.
[02:05] Evan: Quick aside on params — temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling, and max_tokens caps the response. For deterministic answers set temp to 0. We often recommend 0.2-0.6 for assistants.
[02:45] Priya: What's the default retry strategy for transient errors? We need idempotency for certain prompts.
[02:52] Samantha: Great question. SDKs do exponential backoff by default, but we recommend idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations and to detect partial streams — in streaming you may re-request with the same key and dedupe on client.
[03:20] Jing: On PHI — if we keep data in hosted, how is it handled? We need SOC 2, encryption at rest and in transit, and customer-managed KMS ideally.
[03:33] Evan: We can share SOC 2 and security pack. Hosted API encrypts in transit and at rest; for enterprise we offer customer-managed KMS and Private (VPC) deployments. Also audit logs and RBAC via SSO/SAML.
[04:05] Carlos: Latency—can you get sub-200ms token latency?
[04:11] Samantha: Depends on model and sequence length. For smaller contexts we can hit low latencies on hosted; Dedicated with pinned GPUs can guarantee tighter SLOs. We also have smart routing and caching that help.
[04:45] Evan: Let's demo a streaming example — you'll see token chunks arrive progressively. Note that transcription might show slight typos, but in the app you get streaming JSON chunks.
[05:00] Samantha: (runs code) Starting stream... chunk1: "Hello"... chunk2: "How can I help"... you can wire this into the frontend to show partial tokens.
[05:35] Tom: If a stream fails mid-response, do you have a recommended recovery pattern?
[05:40] Samantha: Best practice: include sequence ids and partial state; on reconnect, either resume from last token if supported or re-call with conversation history and dedupe outputs. Use idempotency keys to avoid double actions.
[06:10] Priya: Show us Console — where do we inspect token usage and latency?
[06:16] Evan: Switching to Console — here's per-route token breakdown, latency percentiles, and a trace. You can filter by model, route, and time window.
[06:40] Samantha: Console also surfaces Optimize recommendations: batching suggestions, KV cache hits, and quantization profiles for cost savings. For chat workloads, prefix caching can save tokens when users start from templates.
[07:15] Carlos: Curious about batching — doesn't batching increase latency?
[07:20] Samantha: There's a trade-off. Batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token; Redwood Optimize gives workload-aware batching config so you can balance latency SLOs with cost. For interactive UIs we use small batch windows or async fallback.
[08:00] Jing: Compliance — is there a way to configure data retention? We need 90-day retention and the ability to purge.
[08:08] Evan: Yes, retention windows are configurable and you can request deletions. For Private deployments you keep everything inside your VPC if you require.
[08:35] Tom: Show an SDK example for retries and streaming in Node.
[08:40] Samantha: (shares code) Here's the Node snippet: create client, call chat.create with stream: true, on data append chunks. For retries, use the SDK's retry middleware or roll your own with backoff and idempotency keys.
[09:20] Priya: Any rate limiting or quotas on hosted?
[09:24] Evan: Yes, we enforce quotas per account; rate limits are configurable for enterprise tiers. We also expose token-level throttles and per-route limits.
[09:50] Carlos: What's the billing model for hosted chat?
[09:53] Evan: Usage-based per token for input and output, plus optional per-request fees for certain models. We'll send a pricing sheet. For Dedicated you sign a reserved capacity contract.
[10:20] Samantha: Back to streaming pitfalls — clients should handle partial JSON tokens, maybe buffer until newline, validate JSON. Also consider fallbacks for slow networks.
[10:50] Tom: You mentioned Optimize — can that surface quantization suggestions automatically?
[10:55] Samantha: Yes, Optimize profiles models based on throughput and accuracy targets; it might recommend 8-bit or 4-bit quantization for cost. But we validate quality with your eval prompts before recommending in production.
[11:30] Priya: For our healthcare assistant, hallucinations are a risk. How do you help with guardrails?
[11:36] Samantha: We provide eval hooks and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. You can create test prompts and monitor quality; Optimize can flag regressions after model rollouts. Also function calling with constrained schema helps reduce hallucination for structured outputs.
[12:10] Evan: Quick demo of an edge case — long context. We show how KV cache keeps key/values to avoid re-sending long system prompts and reduces token cost.
[12:40] Samantha: (demo) Here's an example: when a user resumes a prior thread we pull from KV cache so the model sees less repeated context.
[13:10] Carlos: Any SDKs for Python or Go?
[13:14] Samantha: Yes — official SDKs for Node, Python, Go, and Java, plus REST.
[13:40] Jing: For security review, we'll need a SOC2 report and pen test results. Also want to know if Redwood signs BAAs for PHI.
[13:52] Evan: We have SOC 2 and pen test summaries; BAA is on a case-by-case basis with our legal team — we'll share contacts.
[14:20] Tom: Are there patterns for hybrid—some traffic hosted, some on Dedicated?
[14:24] Samantha: Absolutely. Smart routing lets you route by latency, cost, or data residency. You can set failover to Dedicated or Private.
[14:52] Priya: For a pilot, can we run a performance benchmark?
[14:56] Evan: Yes — we often run a short benchmark with sample prompts and your traffic shape. That helps us recommend model variants and batching configs.
[15:22] Samantha: Now a quick walkthrough of typical request payloads — messages array, system role, user role, optional functions. Here's a sample with streaming headers.
[16:00] Carlos: If we need a lower-latency tail, are there any tricks?
[16:05] Samantha: Use shorter system prompts, prefix caching, and smaller token windows. Also choose model variants optimized for latency; our model catalog labels variants with latency/cost profiles.
[16:40] Tom: Can you demo retry headers and idempotency key usage?
[16:45] Samantha: (shares) Add header X-Idempotency-Key and in SDK call set idempotency to true; for streaming partial failures use resumed sequence tokens.
[17:15] Priya: How about webhooks for async responses?
[17:20] Evan: We support async request patterns where you post a job and get notified via webhook when complete — useful for longer generation tasks.
[17:50] Carlos: Any limits on streaming connections?
[17:54] Samantha: We have connection limits per account but they're high; enterprise tiers get higher concurrency. We'll include those numbers in the security packet.
[18:30] Tom: Are there sample apps or quickstarts?
[18:34] Evan: Yes, we have GitHub quickstarts and reference apps for chat UI and agents. We'll share links.
[19:05] Samantha: One more thing — when you do canary rollouts for model updates, Console shows rollout percentage and you can auto-fallback if metrics degrade.
[19:40] Priya: That helps. For our POC success criteria: 200ms median token latency, <0.5% error rate, and cost under $X per session — we can share exact numbers after this call.
[20:00] Evan: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot plan after we get your sample prompts and traffic pattern.
[20:22] Tom: Any gotchas about tokens counting? For example system messages — are they counted?
[20:26] Samantha: Everything in the request and response tokens count toward billing, including system messages. KV cache can reduce that by avoiding re-sending large system contexts.
[21:00] Carlos: For offline audit, can we stream logs to our SIEM?
[21:05] Evan: Yes, audit logs and traces can be exported; integrations include SIEM and cloud logging.
[21:30] Jing: Encryption — do you have HSM-backed KMS?
[21:34] Evan: Yes for enterprise we support customer-managed keys and HSM integrations.
[22:00] Samantha: Wrapping up the demo — streaming, params, retries, SDK patterns, console insights, and Optimize suggestions. Any other technical deep dives needed now?
[22:15] Priya: We'll need a performance check and security packet. Also want an estimate on cost for a few thousand sessions per day.
[22:25] Evan: Noted. We'll send pricing and security docs.
[22:40] Tom: Timeline — we're aiming for a pilot in 4 weeks, decision in 8-10 weeks.
[22:46] Evan: Perfect. We'll follow-up with materials and propose dates for pilot kickoff.
[23:10] Samantha: Thanks everyone — we'll email the links and next steps.
[23:20] Priya: Thanks, really helpful demo.
[23:25] Evan: Bye all.
next_steps: Send hosted API pricing sheet and model catalog link
Share SOC 2 report, pen test summary, and security packet
Schedule 60-min POC scoping call (pilot plan) in 1 week
Run performance benchmark with NexaHealth sample prompts
